title: Trump Uses Rare 'Pocket Rescission' to Claw Back $1 Billion
summary:
President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending that Congress already approved — using a rare and contested power called a "pocket rescission." The White House announced the move Friday.

Most of the cuts hit Health and Human Services programs serving refugees and unaccompanied minors. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have dropped. Also targeted: a Department of Education program for migrant students, a Justice Department office focused on reducing racial tensions, a minority business development initiative, and housing counseling services. The White House called some grants "outright harmful and blatantly ideological."

Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, condemned the move. She said it came "without warning or consultation" and called it "a usurpation of Congress's appropriations powers." Under federal law, Congress gets 45 days to review proposed cuts. But Trump announced them with only five days left in the fiscal year — and the House is out of session until November. The Government Accountability Office says the maneuver is illegal.

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the committee, called it "theft from the American people, plain and simple." The White House argues the tool is legally permissible. A year ago, Trump used a pocket rescission for the first time in nearly 50 years, blocking $4.9 billion in foreign aid. The Supreme Court declined to block it. This time, the target is domestic spending — and the fight over presidential power is heading back to the courts. Because the House is out of session, Congress may not be able to vote to reject the cuts before the 45-day review window closes, leaving the money permanently unspent. That is why the maneuver is called a pocket rescission: the cuts take effect while lawmakers are away. Critics say this lets the president override Congress's power over spending, which the Constitution gives to the legislative branch. Supporters say the law allows it, and the courts will decide who is right.
why_it_matters: This fight is really about who controls the federal budget — the president or Congress — and the outcome could set a precedent for how much money a president can redirect on his own, affecting programs from refugee services to student support.

background_read: Making a law in the United States takes two branches: Congress (the Senate and the House of Representatives, which write laws and approve spending) decides how federal money is used, while the president runs the agencies that spend it. The Constitution gives Congress this 'power of the purse,' meaning the president cannot simply decide on his own not to spend money lawmakers voted for.

That rule was tested in the 1970s, when President Richard Nixon refused to release billions of dollars Congress had appropriated. The result was the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which lets a president propose canceling spending but gives Congress a limited window — the 45 days mentioned in this story — to accept or reject the request.

A 'pocket rescission' exploits that window: if the request is sent so late that lawmakers cannot vote in time, the money expires unspent. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) is the federal watchdog that checks whether agencies follow spending law, and it has argued this kind of maneuver is not allowed.
Because the two branches disagree about what the law permits, courts — not voters — usually end up settling these fights; last year the Supreme Court declined to block a similar move.

perspectives.description: The administration says the money is no longer needed because illegal border crossings have dropped, and that some grants were 'outright harmful and blatantly ideological.' It argues the rescission tool is legally permissible and that courts will confirm it.

Sen. Collins calls it a 'usurpation' done 'without warning or consultation,' and Sen. Murray calls it 'theft from the American people.' The GAO says the maneuver is illegal because it sidesteps the 45-day review Congress is supposed to get.

Presidents of both parties have tested the line between proposing cuts and refusing to spend money, ever since the Nixon-era fights that produced the 1974 Impoundment Control Act. This is the latest round in a decades-long tug-of-war over the power of the purse.

If courts uphold the maneuver, future presidents of either party gain a stronger hand over spending; if they strike it down, Congress may rewrite the timing rules for rescission requests. Either way, programs cut now would have to be refunded later — if Congress chooses to act.
